task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to measure adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended mix?
Is there enough statistical power with 54 series to detect a plausible winning effect?
Can team-quality confounding be adequately controlled?
Does the recommended mix leak future information into adherence measures?

historical_evidence.finding: Game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confound). Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered; ~80 series needed for p<0.05). Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% vs 25-50% bin 37.0%. Confounded by team quality (e.g. OKC disciplined and good).
Avg |delta| between observed and recommended mix on leverage buckets 4.5pp to 24.0pp; 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1. No outcome comparison; single-game horizon; descriptive only.

Full-tier Spearman rho=-0.0639, p=0.099717 (no clear full-rank signal). Pairwise BEST vs AVOID significant (Mann-Whitney p=0.004018). Trigger accuracy rho=0.4525. Average counter n=6.9 possessions. Leakage and low measurement reliability noted.
Series winners LLM-inferred (0/2073 calls to lookup); low-n claims (e.g., 0.0 PPP on n=3); MIA-BOS G7 score invented. Artifact from LLM construction, not genuine outcome data.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level Spearman correlation of AVOID share with winning
failed_approaches.why: Underpowered (n=50, need ~80) and confounded by team quality; question deemed unanswerable with that design.
Large gaps between observed and recommended mix (4.5–24 percentage points); no outcome comparison; small sample (4 games).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Full-tier Spearman validation of playsheet counter ranking
failed_approaches.why: Not significant; limited by leakage, low measurement reliability (avg counter n=6.9 possessions), and small sample.

evidence_establishes: Simple correlations between avoidance shares and winning are confounded by team quality and underpowered at the series level (SF-[prior work]).
Adherence to a recommended opener is far from perfect; observed gaps of 4.5–24 percentage points exist even in a descriptive sample (SF-[prior work]).
The counter-ranking system shows some pairwise signal (BEST > AVOID) but the full ranking is noisy and not conventionally significant (SF-[prior work]).
Outcome labels must be looked up from real data; LLM-inferred winners produce artifacts (SF-[prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a well-controlled adherence measure (not raw AVOID share) can predict winning above chance.
The minimum sample size needed for a properly powered test of adherence vs. winning, given measurement noise and clustering.
How much of the adherence–winning relationship survives controlling for team pre-series strength, rest, and matchup quality.
Whether the recommended mix itself is stable across seasons or drifts (non-stationarity).
own_inferences: The question as posed requires defining 'adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix' – likely a continuous compliance score – and testing its association with series (or game) wins.

The only available unit is 54 series; the most similar prior analysis needed ~80 series for marginal significance, so power will be insufficient unless the effect is large or the analysis uses game-level observations (still clustered).
Measurement reliability is a severe bottleneck: [prior work] shows observed mix differs substantially from recommendation, so any adherence score will be noisy.

If recommendations are derived from the same series data used to evaluate winning, lookahead leakage is a near-certainty; cross-validation or explicit out-of-sample recommendation generation would be required.

Even if adherence could be measured reliably, team quality confounds any season-level relationship (better teams both win more and may show more disciplined adherence). Game-level within-series analyses cannot fully eliminate this unless opponent-adjusted.
uncertainties: Exact definition of 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' – is it the opener rank, the full mix, or a binary 'follow best' indicator?
How adherence should be aggregated across games and possessions (sum, mean, threshold).
Whether additional years of data (2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25) contain the necessary play-type tagging and matchup data to construct recommendations retrospectively.
The true underlying effect size, if any, is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Before retrieval, the feasibility was uncertain. [prior work] show that the closest prior attempt (AVOID share vs winning) was underpowered and confounded; adherence measurement is large-gap even descriptively; and the counter-ranking signal is too noisy to support a robust test. These findings collectively shift the prior from unknown to do_not_proceed, because the known risks (sample size power, measurement reliability, confounding) are severe and unlikely to be overcome with the current data (54 series).

blocking_constraints.text: 54 series is below the ~80 needed for a moderate effect (SF-[prior work]); game-level analysis would increase N but introduce within-series dependence and still be underpowered for a small adherence effect.
Execution conformance gaps of 4.5–24 pp (SF-[prior work]) imply any adherence metric is noisy; the counter ranking itself is not reliably ordered (SF-[prior work]).
Team quality confounds both winning and likely adherence, as noted in SF-[prior work]; without a credible team-quality control (e.g., pre-series Elo) the relationship cannot be interpreted.

prior_work.summary: Two families directly tested related hypotheses (AVOID share vs winning, ranking validation) and were inconclusive/untestable due to small sample and confounding. A third showed adherence measurement gaps. None established that suppressing-conditional recommended mix adherence predicts winning.

risks.text: Only 54 series are available; prior work required ~80 series for a correlation of similar magnitude. A series-level test will be underpowered.
Better teams both win more and may adhere more to recommendations; uncontrolled team quality can produce spurious positive association.
Adherence to a recommended mix is not uniform; average gaps of 4.5–24 percentage points were observed in a small sample, and the full counter ranking is noisy (Spearman p=0.10).

If the recommended mix is derived from the same series used to evaluate winning (e.g., suppression observed in early games used to predict later wins), lookahead leakage is possible. Must use only prior data or strict out-of-sample partitioning.
Adherence scores may have a mechanical floor (e.g., forced deviations in dead-ball and transition possessions) that weakens signal.
The suppression model and optimal mix may change between seasons or playoff rounds, invalidating pooled historical comparisons.

design.estimand: Causal or partial correlation between a per-game adherence score (how well the offense's observed play-type mix aligns with the suppression-conditional recommended opener ranking) and the probability of winning that game, controlling for pre-game team quality and game context.
design.unit: playoff game, nested in series and season
design.sample: All playoff games from seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 for which complete play-type tagging, matchup data, and a pre-computed suppression-conditional recommended mix are available. Approximately 250–300 games across ~54 series.
design.power: Simulation-based power analysis required; given clustering and likely small effect, series-level analysis is underpowered (need ~80 series). A game-level analysis with clustered standard errors may achieve 80% power for an odds ratio of ~1.2 if adherence variance is sufficient, but the noise in adherence measurement reduces effective N. A pilot calibration on the first half of series is recommended before committing.
design.controls: Pre-series team strength (rolling Elo, net rating), home-court advantage, rest days, series score entering the game, and season fixed effects. In sensitivity analyses, opponent-adjusted team quality (opponent Elo differential).
design.falsification: (1) Test whether adherence in garbage-time possessions (last 5 min with win probability ≥95%) predicts winning; null expected. (2) Shuffle the recommended ranking within each game to create a placebo adherence score and test its association with winning. (3) Use pre-series data to check whether teams that tend to adhere more in the regular season also adhere more in playoffs, verifying that adherence is a stable trait rather than a response to winning situations.
design.multiplicity: Bonferroni correction if multiple adherence thresholds or play-type subsets are tested. Specify the primary adherence metric (e.g., fraction of possessions where observed play type matches the top-ranked recommended opener) before seeing data.
design.decision_rule: p < 0.05 (two-sided) for the primary game-level logistic regression coefficient on adherence, with cluster-robust standard errors by series. Reject if coefficient is not distinguishable from zero; treat as suggestive if nominal p < 0.05 but not surviving multiplicity correction.
design.data_version: NBA play-by-play seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26, processed with [source] database schema as of 2026-06-16. Play-type initiation records from Neo4j INITIATED [source]; suppression model version and recommended mix algorithm locked before analysis.
